title: The CAP Theorem
sources: Wikipedia, 'CAP theorem' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CAP_theorem): a distributed data store can provide only two of consistency (every read receives the most recent write or an error), availability (every request received by a non-failing node gets a non-error response) and partition tolerance (the system keeps working despite messages being dropped or delayed between nodes); when a network partition happens you must choose between consistency and availability. Conjectured by Eric Brewer (2000), proved by Seth Gilbert and Nancy Lynch (2002)

Brewer, 'CAP Twelve Years Later: How the Rules Have Changed' (IEEE Computer, 2012): the '2 of 3' formulation is misleading; partitions are rare but cannot be avoided in a distributed system, so the real choice is between C and A only while a partition is happening

Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications, ch. 9: network faults happen whether you like it or not, so the choice is 'either Consistent or Available when Partitioned'; a system that refuses requests during a partition keeps consistency, one that answers from a possibly out-of-date replica stays available

lines.text: Yesterday we split our data across machines.
But what if they stop talking?
That's where the Cap theorem comes in.
C: consistency, everyone sees the latest data.
A: availability, every request gets an answer.
P: partition tolerance, surviving a broken network.
Picture two pizza branches sharing one menu,
when the phone line between them gets cut.
A customer asks for today's price.
Give a maybe-old price, and you stay available,
or say try again later, and you stay consistent.
During a cut, you can't have both.
A bank would rather wait, a like counter would rather answer.
